claims.claim: Front/back/rounding/raising definitions and diphthong quantity; macrons mark length, not all weight.
Local j, reconstruction-star and historical-arrow conventions; distinguish source-printed earlier forms from coexisting paradigms.
Earlier stressed short a-fronting except the nasal environment and later restoration before w or a following back vowel in an open syllable.
Breaking concerns stressed vowels, begins from immediate æ/e/i inputs and has vowel-specific conditions; rj excluded, rr included, e-before-l restricted, i-before-l not securely established.
The earlier preterite *hælp broke before lp while helpan did not; eald shows æ before ld.
Breaking preserves the short/long distinction; some long vowels broke before h; later West Saxon io/eo merger prevents an inverse spelling rule.
Historical front mutation anticipates following i/j, frequently lost later; the selected result table is bounded, including the separate nasal-vowel history.
fēt is nominative/accusative plural and selected dative singular; front mutation is not a general plural marker.
The earlier weak-verb formation *dōm(i)jan provides the conditioning j behind dēman beside dōm.
eald/ieldra/ieldest combines earlier breaking and later mutation; the comparison identifies stems, not new complete paradigms.
hātan/hǣtt illustrates present-singular front mutation; helpan/hilpð reflects older e-raising; ēo/īe has a multistage history.
West Saxon initial-palatal diphthongization affects a following stressed vowel, is distinct from consonant palatalization and follows breaking; geat/gatu reflects earlier vowel histories.
The coexisting giefan principal parts preserve short geaf versus long gēafon.
Back mutation affects a stressed short front vowel and has West Saxon restrictions on intervening consonants and the following vowel; later io/eo merger and analogy affect the visible distribution.
heofon/hefon is an original comparison of two source-printed forms, not Fulk’s literal parenthetic pair; hefon has visible access to heofon.
Late West Saxon smoothing and Anglian smoothing have distinct conditions; hēah/hēh is explicitly labelled Late West Saxon and spelling inconsistent.
Palatalization responds to the older environment; *kōljan explains the hard c of cēlan despite its later front vowel.
Following j can geminate a consonant after a light syllable, with r excepted; Gothic bidjan is a cognate of biddan, not its parent.
Apocope/syncope, vowel length and weight are defined distinctly; hof/hofu, word/word and wīf/wīf illustrate bounded final high-vowel loss.
hēafod/hēafdes shows syncope; hēafodes is an analogically restored fuller form, with explicit headword access.
Intervocalic h-loss precedes contraction in *seohan/sēon, contrasting seoh; compensatory lengthening has distinct environments.
Inherited ablaut and later changes together shape principal parts; umlaut does not generate a strong preterite.
cweðan/cweden exemplifies inherited consonant alternation, with Verner’s law predating fixed Germanic stress; ordinary OE fricative voicing is distinct.
Analogy can restore, extend or remove alternations; actual paradigms remain the authority for attested forms.
Summary consolidates the qualified mechanisms already explained and gives exact source-note locators, rather than introducing new histories.
